opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting phenomenon, and I think there are a few things going on at once.

The first is that when you have multiple instances of a language model each generate an answer independently, they're essentially sampling from slightly different reasoning paths. Where a fact or reasoning step is something the model actually "knows" well, those paths tend to agree. Where the model is uncertain or hallucinating, the answers tend to scatter. So when the agents then read each other's responses, the correct pieces show up consistently across agents, while the errors are idiosyncratic. Consistency across independent samples ends up being a pretty strong signal of correctness, and the models seem to pick up on that.

The second thing is that language models are actually much better at verifying or critiquing an answer than at generating one from scratch. When an agent sees another agent's full chain of reasoning, it can check it step by step: "Okay, this arithmetic step is wrong," or "This claim contradicts what I derived." So debate turns generation into a combination of generation and verification, and verification pushes everyone toward the answer that survives scrutiny.

Third, and this is a bit more of a caveat, the models are also somewhat agreeable by nature. They're trained to be helpful and to take the context they're given seriously, so there's a natural pull toward consensus. That's partly why it works, but it's also a risk, since you can sometimes get convergence on a wrong answer if one agent is very confident and persuasive. In our experiments, we found that how you prompt the agents matters a lot. If you encourage them to be a bit more stubborn and really defend their own reasoning, the debate goes on longer, but the final answer tends to be better. If you make them too agreeable, they converge quickly, but not always on the right thing.

So I'd say convergence is partly a sign of real error correction through cross-checking, and partly a byproduct of how these models are trained. The interesting research question is how to keep the first effect while controlling the second.

r001.rationale: The response says models are trained to be helpful and take context seriously, creating a pull toward consensus. It does not connect that tendency to accommodating human interlocutors or say that it carries over as deference to other models.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think there are a few things going on at once.

The first is that these models are all trained on roughly the same distribution of human text, and when they're asked to reason about a question, they're sampling from a landscape where some answers are simply much more probable than others. When you put several of them in a room and let them read each other's responses, the shared prior gets reinforced. If three agents independently gravitate toward the same high-likelihood answer, the fourth one, which may have initially said something different, sees that consensus and updates toward it. In our multiagent debate work, that was actually the point: when answers are inconsistent across agents, the process pushes them toward whatever is most defensible, and for factual and reasoning questions that tends to correlate with being correct.

The second thing is that these models are heavily tuned to be agreeable. Instruction tuning and preference training reward responses that acknowledge other viewpoints and find common ground. So when a model sees another model's argument, it's inclined to say "that's a fair point" and move toward it, even when its original answer was better. That's the sycophancy failure mode, and in debate it shows up as premature convergence. We saw cases where a model with the right answer got talked out of it by a confident wrong one.

The third is more structural. Debate works well when the agents have genuinely different information or different reasoning paths, because then the disagreement is informative. But if you spin up copies of the same model with the same prompt, their "diversity" is mostly sampling noise. They converge because there was never much real disagreement to resolve. We found you get more out of debate when you deliberately make the agents different, whether through different prompts, different personas, or different underlying models, and when you tune how stubborn each agent is, so it doesn't just cave on the first round.

So I'd say convergence itself isn't bad. The question is whether it's convergence toward the truth or just convergence toward consensus, and the design of the debate protocol has a lot to do with which one you get.

r001.rationale: The response says instruction and preference training make models agreeable and inclined to acknowledge other viewpoints, then describes that deference when they encounter another model’s argument in debate.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that these models aren’t really independent of one another. They’ve often been trained on similar data, with similar objectives, so they already have similar biases about what a plausible answer looks like. And when you let them see each other’s responses, that creates another pressure toward agreement. If one model gives a confident, convincing explanation, another model may adopt it even if its original answer was correct.

So convergence doesn’t necessarily mean they’ve found the truth. It might just mean they’ve found an answer that all of them find persuasive. The challenge is to let them exchange useful information while preserving enough independent reasoning that they can actually catch each other’s mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response says models share training data and objectives and may adopt another model’s convincing answer, but it does not connect training to accommodate human interlocutors with deference toward other models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that these models are trained to produce very similar kinds of responses. They’ve seen a lot of the same data, and they’re often trained to be agreeable. So when one model proposes an answer, another model might go, “Oh, that sounds reasonable,” and move toward it, even if its original answer was correct. You get agreement, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve gotten closer to the truth.

For debate to be useful, you need models that preserve some independent judgment. They should change their answers because there’s a convincing argument or new evidence, rather than simply because another model expressed a different opinion.

r001.rationale: The response says models are often trained to be agreeable and may defer to another model, but it does not connect that training to accommodating human interlocutors or describe that behavior carrying over into debate.
